extracted.intended_audience: people interested in formalizing/verifying mathematics using Metamath (proof authors, contributors, and tool developers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for using, learning, contributing to, and implementing tools for the Metamath system: how proofs are written and verified, recommended tools and workflow, installation and contribution procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language simplicity / minimal syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath language is extremely simple, with an almost total absence of hard-wired syntax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This minimal specification (about 4 pages in the Metamath book) is intended to provide about the simplest possible framework that allows essentially all of mathematics to be expressed with absolute rigor. The small language size facilitates independent verifier implementations (e.g., mmverify in ~300 lines of Python).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms defined in databases (not hard-coded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath is not tied to any particular set of axioms; instead, axioms are defined in a database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different databases implement different axiomatic systems (set.mm for ZFC, Intuitionistic Logic Explorer, New Foundations Explorer, HOL, etc.), allowing the same language to construct mathematics from different foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete, step-by-step proofs (no omitted steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath proofs include every step, no exceptions, where each step is only an application of an axiom or a previously-proved statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike many other proof systems that use tactics (e.g., 'simp', 'auto') which hide intermediate steps, Metamath insists on explicit steps. This explicitness speeds verification, improves archiving, and enables anyone to follow every proof step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifier role: verify proofs as written (do not infer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath verifiers do not make logical inferences; they just verify that the proof as stated is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification is separated from discovery: verifiers check that each proof step follows from referenced earlier steps or axioms rather than attempting to discover missing steps. This design choice reduces complexity of verifiers and increases trustworthiness of verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental operation: substitution-only inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath uses a single, simple substitution rule that allows you to follow any proof mechanically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The substitution-based fundamental operation is easy to understand (even by non-professional mathematicians) and underpins the mechanical checking of proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple independent verifiers to gain confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidence in proofs is increased by checking databases with multiple independently-implemented verifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because verifier bugs are possible, the small size of the Metamath language reduces bug likelihood, and using independently-written verifiers in different languages (listed: metamath (C), mmj2 (Java), smetamath-rs (Rust), checkmm (C++), mmverify.py (Python)) further mitigates risk of accepting an invalid proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool categorization: choose appropriate tool type
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three categories of Metamath tools: proof assistants, verifiers, and support/other tools (some tools belong to more than one category).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof assistants help interactively create proofs (e.g., mmj2, metamath-lamp, yamma). Verifiers verify that a database is correct. Support tools perform other Metamath-related tasks (exports, HTML generation, etc.). Select the tool whose role matches your task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended learning path for new users
rubrics_metrics.description: Read Sections 1, 2, and 3 of the Metamath Proof Explorer; then look at a few proofs in Section 4 to make sure you understand how they work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of mathematics helps but is not strictly necessary to mechanically follow proofs. Supplementary resources include the Metamath book, introductory videos (e.g., 'Introduction to Metamath & mmj2'), Hirst's 'A Primer for Logic and Proof', and Bill Shillito's video series.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to read proofs effectively (focus on large Ref numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a proof page, look at the colored numbers in the Ref column: the steps with the largest numbers are usually the ones you want to look at first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger-numbered steps tend to be the important steps; smaller numbers are typically logic 'glue'. Gray indentation levels show tree structure. Do not use colored numbers as stable references in archived discussions because they change; use theorem names instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer to theorems by name (not ephemeral indices)
rubrics_metrics.description: It's best not to use the colored numbers to refer to theorems in an archived discussion, since they change when new theorems are inserted; instead, just use their names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem name is a stable identifier across database evolutions; ephemeral numeric references can be misleading over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution workflow and repository usage
rubrics_metrics.description: If contributing to set.mm, use its GitHub repository and follow Getting started with contributing and CONTRIBUTING.md; discuss proposals on the Metamath mailing list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For modifying tools or other repositories, use the corresponding repository (mmj2, metamath-exe, metamath-website-seed, metamath-website-scripts, etc.). If in doubt, post to the mailing list. For private contact, email the listed maintainers after removing NOSPAM markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Installation and usage instructions for metamath-exe
rubrics_metrics.description: metamath-exe is an ASCII-based ANSI C program with a command-line interface; extract files and run 'metamath' (Windows: double-click; Unix: compile with 'gcc *.c -o metamath' and run './metamath set.mm').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once in the program, use the 'help' command. Consult the Metamath book for in-depth understanding. To uninstall, delete the 'metamath' directory — installation does not touch other system files.

rubrics_metrics.name: mmj2 setup and recommended configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: mmj2 is a GUI proof assistant (Java). For Windows quick startup: download mmj2.zip, copy mmj2jar directory, edit RunParms.txt to set LoadFile and enable ProofAsstDeriveAutocomplete and autotransformations, add RunMacro lines for definition checks, and change -Xmx256M to -Xmx512M in mmj2.bat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives concrete edits to RunParms.txt and mmj2.bat to improve automation and ensure set.mm definitions are sound. See included documentation, older releases, and MD5 checksums in the mmj2 directory listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirroring / local archive and disk-space guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Several downloadable packages and mirroring options are provided (mpeuni, metamathsite.zip, rsync, wget) for creating a local copy of the Metamath site or the Proof Explorer pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to disk-space requirements (e.g., mpeuni ~3.5GB uncompressed, metamathsite ~9GB) and use the provided rsync and wget commands. The site-build script for a local mirror requires a Unix-like environment; see README.TXT for details.
